description:
Across space, silent machines stand as reminders of humanity's greatest adventures. Once our eyes, ears and explorers on distant worlds, these remarkable pieces of engineering have transmitted their final messages. But what became of them?

We are Lost in Transmission! Through creative storytelling, we're uncovering the extraordinary stories behind the machines we sent to live among the stars. Because every machine has a story worth telling. Even after its last transmission.
summary:
Lost in Transmission is an interactive website told from the perspective of NASA’s final command to the Opportunity rover – the last message sent from Earth on 12 February 2019, asking it to beep. Visitors become that signal. Guided by a mission map, they travel to Mars, meeting the silent explorers along the way – Viking 1 and Spirit – to discover what each machine was, what it found, and how its mission ended. Finally, they reach Opportunity in Perseverance Valley… and wait for a reply that never comes. The story ends with Perseverance, which continues the work today.

The challenge asks for a story that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to NASA hardware left on Mars. Designed for ages 12–13, our project turns NASA mission data, photos and records into short, typed storytelling with interactive moments – like watching Opportunity’s real last image stop loading halfway. Every fact and image comes from NASA and JPL.

Young people often hear only about active missions. By giving these machines a voice, we aim to create a personal connection to the robotic explorers that paved the way for today’s missions, and inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers.
details:
Lost in Transmission
You are NASA’s last message to Opportunity. Cross the solar system, meet the silent explorers of Mars, and find out why no one answered.

What it does
Lost in Transmission is an interactive website told from the perspective of NASA’s final command to the Opportunity rover, the last message sent from Earth on 12 February 2019, asking it to beep. Visitors become that signal. They travel across space to Mars, passing Opportunity’s predecessors along the way to discover what each machine was, what it found and how its mission ended. Finally, they reach Opportunity in Perseverance Valley… and wait for a reply that never comes.

How it works
Users are transported to Mars and guided by illuminated buttons and a mission map, which shows the journey ahead and gives a sense of adventure, as if they are completing a mission. The journey visits Viking 1, Spirit and Opportunity, and ends with Perseverance, which continues the work today. Players can jump to any checkpoint except Opportunity, which unlocks only after the earlier stages so its ending lands with full emotional weight.

Each stop tells its story through short, typed text with deliberate pauses, real NASA photographs, labelled rover diagrams and the discoveries each machine made. At Opportunity, a pulsing “Waiting for signal…” bar is followed by “No reply.” Opportunity’s real last image then loads and stops halfway, just as it did for NASA in 2018. NASA’s official farewell video follows, showing behind-the-scenes views and the real reactions of the team. The story ends with Perseverance, turning a goodbye into a handover.

Benefits and intended impact
School-age space enthusiasts often hear only about active missions. This project gives the silent machines of Mars a voice and turns dense technical records into a story that 12–13-year-olds can follow and feel. Beyond informing, the aim is to give audiences a personal connection to these machines and inspire the next generation of space enthusiasts, showing that each mission paved the way for the next.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages
  • The team built the main HTML structure, layout and styling, and made all design decisions. Claude Code (Anthropic) was used for the more complex tasks, such as typing animations, signal effects and image reveals. Claude helped with research, fact-checking and simplifying the text.
  • NASA and JPL mission pages, photojournal images, press releases and technical reports
  • NASA Goddard Scientific Visualization Studio’s Deep Star Maps 2020 for the background, which uses ESA Gaia DR2 data

What makes it creative
Instead of a fact sheet, the visitor is part of the story: the final command itself. The emotion comes from interaction, not just text: waiting for a reply, watching a real image fail to arrive, and unlocking the ending only after getting to know the rovers that came before.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every fact was checked against NASA and JPL sources. For example, we avoided the popular quote “My battery is low and it’s getting dark”, because it was a reporter’s paraphrase, not a real message.
  • Age group: short sentences, one idea per screen, and pauses that give readers time to take things in.
  • Image rights: all images are NASA media, credited on screen, with no NASA logos used.
  • Emotional pacing: I built up to Opportunity’s silence and ended on hope with Perseverance.
  • Accessibility: readable contrast, and options to skip animations.

What’s next
I’d like to develop the story into an in-person immersive experience: a tunnel of light where visitors become the final command, passing through five rooms with replica rovers, Martian landscapes and video walls, and ending with Perseverance’s successful landing.
